content: 1. Health workers are urgently called to action to address tuberculosis (TB) and related challenges, as highlighted in the International Journal of Tuberculosis and Lung Disease. 2. A study by Sharma et al. compared the tuberculin skin test (TST) and interferon-gamma release assays (IGRAs) for diagnosing latent TB infection in high TB-burden settings, published in PLoS One. 3. Zwerling et al. developed the BCG World Atlas, a comprehensive database of global Bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG) vaccination policies and practices, as detailed in PLoS Medicine in 2011. 4. The 2022 WHO guidelines introduced TB antigen-based skin tests (TBSTs) as a conditional recommendation for TB infection testing, though the evidence supporting this is of very low certainty. 5. Either TST or IGRAs can be used to test for TB infection, with a strong recommendation despite very low certainty of evidence. This was incorporated into the 2022 guidelines as Recommendation 2. 6. IGRAs should not replace TST in lowand middle-income countries for diagnosing latent TB infection in children and adolescents, regardless of HIV status, or for the diagnostic work-up of suspected active TB in these populations. This supersedes the 2011 recommendation. 7. IGRAs should not replace TST in lowand middle-income countries for diagnosing latent TB infection in individuals living with HIV. This is a strong recommendation in the 2022 guidelines, replacing the 2011 guidance. 8. IGRAs should not be used in health care worker screening programs in lowand middle-income countries. This is a strong recommendation in the 2022 guidelines, replacing the 2011 recommendation. 9. IGRAs should not replace TST in lowand middle-income countries for screening latent TB infection in adult and pediatric contacts or during outbreak investigations. This is a strong recommendation in the 2022 guidelines, replacing the 2011 recommendation. 10. Neither IGRAs nor TST should be used in lowand middle-income countries to identify individuals at risk of developing active TB. This is a strong recommendation in the 2022 guidelines, replacing the 2011 recommendation. 11. IGRAs and TST should not be used in lowand middle-income countries for diagnosing pulmonary or extrapulmonary TB or for the diagnostic work-up of adults, including those living with HIV, suspected of active TB. This is a strong recommendation in the 2022 guidelines. 12. The WHO Guideline Development Group (GDG) and External Review Group (ERG) followed a structured process for decision-making, including drafting PICO questions, assessing evidence, and reaching consensus or voting when necessary. 13. The GDG meetings in 2010 and 2018 were conducted in person, while the 2022 meetings were held virtually due to COVID-19-related travel restrictions. Economic analyses and evidence assessments were presented during introductory webinars. 14. Conflicts of interest (COI) were assessed for all GDG and ERG members. Members were required to submit declarations of interest (DOI) forms, which were reviewed by the WHO steering committee to identify potential conflicts. 15. Significant COIs, such as intellectual bias, financial interests exceeding $5000, or involvement in related research, were evaluated, and management plans were implemented if necessary. Developers of diagnostic assays were excluded from policy development. 16. The names and biographies of GDG members were published on the WHO website for public notice and comment before meetings. Selected individuals with intellectual or research involvement were invited as technical resource persons but excluded from recommendation deliberations. 17. The WHO steering group prepared draft policy guidance based on consensus recommendations, which were reviewed by the GDG and ERG before finalization. 18. The WHO guidelines emphasize the importance of transparency and rigorous evaluation of COIs to ensure the integrity of the guideline development process. 19. Specific GDG members declared interests related to TB diagnostics, such as grants or in-kind support from organizations like QIAGEN and Delft Diagnostics. These were judged not to conflict significantly with the objectives of the guidelines. 20. The WHO guidelines on TB testing and diagnostics reflect a comprehensive and evidence-based approach to addressing TB infection, with a focus on lowand middle-income countries and vulnerable populations.
